extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary/cultural criticism; writers and artists interested in gender and aesthetic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Normative critical criteria about how masculinity/femininity shape art and artistic institutions, and what constitutes healthy artistic practice (applied art, painting, music, dance, architecture, sculpture, literature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art is Human
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is a social process above sex; neither the masculine nor the feminine has any place in Art — the true artist transcends his or her sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance: "Neither the masculine nor the feminine has any place in art--Art is Human. The true artist transcends his sex, or her sex. If this is not the case, the art suffers." The author treats this as a central evaluative principle: art should be judged by its human/social quality, not by sex-specific expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose egoistic / self-expressive art
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive self-expression (an essentially masculine impulse) disfigures art; art should be social expression rather than the artist's personal outcry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context and examples: masculinity brings "desire, combat, self-expression" and the last, self-expression, is "the main evil" in art. "Miles and miles of poetry consist of the ceaseless outcry of the male for the female..." The work should avoid being simply personal venting and instead aim at communal or social expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applied art should be widespread and pleasurable
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied art ought to be a human function common to everyone — beauty should be made and appreciated in ordinary objects and clothing, giving pleasure to both maker and user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/examples: the cook decorating a pie, textile arts, and clothing should produce a condition "where every human being was a pleasure to the eye, appropriately and beautifully clothed." Applied art at a higher general level is preferable to a narrow elite 'pure art' separated from daily life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should be accessible, not an occult profession
rubrics_metrics.description: Art ought not to become an esoteric, jargon-filled profession inaccessible to the general public; over-specialization and an exclusive critical jargon are negative developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted critique: "Pure art, a fine-spun specialty, a process carried on by an elect few who openly despise the unappreciative many... evolving a jargon of criticism which becomes more esoteric yearly." The implication: evaluate artistic systems negatively when they isolate art from popular appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance masculine and feminine elements in culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Male domination in social life and artistic profession has impoverished art and taste; allowing women equal development would raise artistic standards and the public's aesthetic level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage: men "by refusing the same growth to women, they have not only weakened and reduced the output, but ruined the market as it were, hopelessly and permanently kept down the level of taste." The criterion is inclusivity and balance: the cultural health of art requires women's full participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing should be broadly human, not sexualized display
rubrics_metrics.description: Dancing ought to express broad human communal elements and emotion through the body; when sex-display predominates, dancing is degraded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and contrast: early tribal and Greek dances as social celebration vs modern trend where "the sex-element more and more emphasized" produces the degrading figure of the 'dancing girl' and social dances that become "a pleasant form of dalliance." Good dancing emphasizes varied beauty of posture and expression rather than exhibitionism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture should express needs of women and children
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic architecture should be organized around natural social relations — in particular the needs of women and children (the nursery, daily life) — rather than as an industrial form serving male proprietorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual support: "The home is essentially a place for the woman and the child; yet the needs of woman and child are not expressed in our domestic architecture... The house is the physical expression of the limitations of women; and as such it fills the world with a small drab ugliness." Good architecture concretely expresses simple, human relations and contributes to beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture requires free womanhood and honest standards of the body
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture's development is hindered by degraded conceptions of the human body and restrictive sexual modesty; a 'nobly equal womanhood' and freer standards of beauty/decency would improve sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's claim: sculpture is checked by 'the degradation of the human body, the vicious standards of sex-consciousness enforced under the name of modesty' and hence needs freer womanhood and higher standards to flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music and poetry should avoid one-sided masculine egoism
rubrics_metrics.description: Music and poetry are harmed by excessive masculine passion and egoism; they should move toward social/human expression and be enriched by women's perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support: "Music is injured by a one-sided handling, partly in the excess of the one dominant masculine passion, partly by the general presence of egoism... and this is true also of poetry." The arrival of more women writers is expected to introduce a broader 'human note.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive/decorative female arts are valuable but limited in scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Early decorative arts (pottery, weaving, needlework, embroidery) created by women are often strong and beautiful but belong to applied/primitive art; they are not the same as "Art with a large A," which evolved later as a professional specialty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage: women originated pottery, basketry, needlework, etc., which are 'strong and beautiful, but its time is long past.' The criterion distinguishes the value of domestic/decorative craft from the later professional arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art needs popular appreciation to sustain makers
rubrics_metrics.description: For art to thrive, makers must be upheld and rewarded by popular appreciation; specialist artists depend on a cultivated social appreciation for their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual support: "The maker of beauty is upheld and rewarded by a popular appreciation of her work--or his." The book argues that when appreciation is widespread, both applied and pure arts advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masculine traits that skew art: desire, combat, self-expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Three characteristics commonly attributed to maleness—desire, combat, and self-expression—have shaped art; while desire and combat alter subject and tone, self-expression particularly distorts art away from social aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the text: "As soon as the male of our species assumed the exclusive right to perform all social functions, he necessarily brought to that performance the advantages--and disadvantages--of maleness, of those dominant characteristics, desire, combat, self-expression." The guidance is to recognize these forces when critiquing artistic forms.
